payload.rationale: I assign a 52% probability using a broad historical-growth prior, not a current-quarter nowcast. No contemporaneous economic evidence was supplied. As a transfer assumption, US quarterly real GDP growth at a seasonally adjusted annualized rate is plausibly centered in the low-2% range, with substantial quarter-to-quarter variation. That puts this threshold near the middle of the plausible distribution, offering only a slight lean toward YES. The event requires the BEA’s Q3 2026 Advance Estimate to show a published one-decimal growth rate of at least 2.1%; 2.0% does not qualify, and subsequent revisions are not the target. The strongest reason this estimate could be too high is that weakening consumption, investment, or employment could have shifted Q3 growth materially below the historical prior. The strongest reason it could be too low is that resilient private demand or favorable inventory and net-export contributions could put growth comfortably above 2%. Those are possibilities, not observed conditions. Without current-quarter data, a stronger directional forecast is not warranted.
limitations: No current research or economic observations were supplied, and no browsing or tools were available.
The estimate transfers broad historical US growth behavior to Q3 2026 without conditioning on the actual 2026 economic environment.
Quarterly GDP can fluctuate because of inventories and trade; the Advance Estimate also carries measurement uncertainty.
Settlement depends on the published one-decimal Advance Estimate, not unrounded growth or revised GDP.
